concepts.title: Quadrature Phase
concepts.one_liner: Quadrature phase is a relationship between pairs of filters that enables measuring local oriented energy and identifying contours independently of their phase.
concepts.content: Pairs of filters can be in a relationship to each other that is called quadrature phase. This relationship is useful for many low-level visual processing tasks. When in quadrature phase, pairs of oriented filters can measure what is called local oriented energy, can identify contours independently of the phase of the contour, and can measure positional changes very accurately.
concepts.motivation_md: This relationship allows vision systems to detect features like edges and textures consistently, regardless of whether the feature is a light-to-dark or dark-to-light transition.
concepts.recap_md:
- Quadrature phase relates pairs of oriented filters for low-level vision tasks. 
- It allows for phase-independent contour detection and local energy measurement. 
- It provides a mechanism for highly accurate measurement of positional changes.

concepts.title: Hilbert Transform
concepts.one_liner: The Hilbert transform relates two functions in the Fourier domain by shifting the phase of positive and negative frequency components by $-j$ and $j$ respectively.
concepts.content: For notational simplicity, quadrature pair filters are described in the time domain, but they extend naturally to two or more dimensions. Consider an even symmetric zero-mean signal, $\ell(t)$, with Fourier transform $\mathscr{L}(\omega)$, where $\mathscr{L}(0)=0$ because the signal is zero-mean. In the Fourier domain, two functions, $\mathscr{L}(\omega)$ and $\mathscr{L}_h(\omega)$, are said to be Hilbert transform pairs if: $$\mathscr{L}_h(\omega) = \begin{cases} ~ - j \mathscr{L}(\omega) & \quad \text{if } \omega >0 \\ j \mathscr{L}(\omega) & \quad \text{if } \omega <0 \\ \end{cases}$$ We now define the complex signal: $$\ell_a(t) = \ell(t) + j \ell_h(t)$$
concepts.motivation_md: The Hilbert transform is used to create a complex 'analytic' version of a real signal, allowing for the separation of instantaneous amplitude and phase.
concepts.recap_md:
- A Hilbert transform pair consists of a signal and its phase-shifted version. 
- In the frequency domain, it applies a $-j$ multiplier to positive frequencies and $j$ to negative frequencies. 
- It is used to construct the complex analytic signal $\ell_a(t)$.

concepts.title: Analytic Signal
concepts.one_liner: The analytic signal is a complex signal formed by a real signal and its Hilbert transform, containing no negative frequency components.
concepts.content: The complex signal is defined as: $$\ell_a(t) = \ell(t) + j \ell_h(t)$$ where $\ell_h(t)$ is the Hilbert transform of $\ell(t)$. The signal $\ell_a(t)$ is called the analytic signal and its Fourier transform has no negative frequency components.
concepts.motivation_md: By removing negative frequencies, the analytic signal provides a mathematically convenient way to calculate local properties like envelope and phase.
concepts.recap_md:
- The analytic signal $\ell_a(t)$ is the sum of a signal and $j$ times its Hilbert transform. 
- It is characterized by having a Fourier transform with zero power at negative frequencies.

concepts.title: Local Amplitude
concepts.one_liner: Local amplitude is the instantaneous magnitude of the complex analytic signal, often used to build image representations invariant to certain structures.
concepts.content: The complex signal $\ell_a(t)$ can be written in polar form: $$\ell_a(t) = a(t) \exp \left( j \, \theta (t) \right)$$ where $a(t)$ is the instantaneous amplitude (local amplitude) and $\theta (t)$ is the instantaneous phase (local phase). This particular representation is common in communications theory, and it has been used to build image representations invariant to certain image structures.
concepts.motivation_md: Local amplitude (or envelope) captures the strength of a signal or feature regardless of its specific phase, which is useful for texture and edge energy detection.
concepts.recap_md:
- Local amplitude $a(t)$ is the magnitude component of the analytic signal in polar form. 
- It provides a measure of signal strength that is invariant to phase.

concepts.title: Local Phase
concepts.one_liner: Local phase measures the angle between real and imaginary signal components, providing information sensitive to image structure but invariant to contrast changes.
concepts.content:
The complex signal $\ell_a(t)$ can be written in polar form: $$\ell_a(t) = a(t) \exp \left( j \, \theta (t) \right)$$ where $a(t)$ is the instantaneous amplitude and $\theta (t)$ is the instantaneous phase (local phase). 

The local phase is a measure of angle between the real and imaginary components (cosine and sine in the case of complex Gabor filters): $$\theta(x,y) = \angle \left[ \ell_h(x,y) + j \ell_q(x,y) \right]$$ where $\theta (x,y)$ is the instantaneous phase. This is another interesting nonlinearity although it is not commonly used in neural networks. Local image phase has been used to estimate motion. This information is invariant to local changes of contrast and it is only sensitive to the local image structure. For oriented, spatial filters, cycling through the phase of the quadrature pair of filters can generate motion along the direction of the phase change.
concepts.motivation_md: Local phase captures structural information (like the exact position of an edge) while remaining robust against global or local lighting and contrast variations.
concepts.recap_md:
- Local phase $\theta(x,y)$ is the angle of the complex analytic signal. 
- It is invariant to contrast changes and sensitive primarily to local image structure. 
- It can be used for motion estimation and generating synthetic motion.

concepts.title: Hilbert Transform for Images
concepts.one_liner: The Hilbert transform is extended to images by defining a specific direction in frequency space to separate positive and negative components.
concepts.content:
The extension of the Hilbert transform to images can be done in several ways. The most common approach in image processing is to define one direction, $n$, in the frequency space and then the Hilbert transform is as follows: 

$$\mathscr{L}_h(\omega_x,\omega_y) = \begin{cases} ~ - j \mathscr{L}(\omega_x,\omega_y) & \quad \text{if } n^T \cdot (\omega_x,\omega_y) > 0 \\ j \mathscr{L}(\omega_x,\omega_y) & \quad \text{if } n^T \cdot (\omega_x,\omega_y) <0 \\ \end{cases}$$
concepts.motivation_md: Extending the Hilbert transform to 2D allows for the calculation of local phase and amplitude in images along specific orientations.
concepts.recap_md:
- The 2D Hilbert transform requires choosing a direction vector $n$ in the frequency domain. 
- It shifts phases based on the sign of the dot product between the frequency coordinates and $n$.

concepts.title: Quadrature Pairs in Band-pass Filters
concepts.one_liner: Two band-pass filters are in quadrature if their impulse responses are Hilbert transform pairs along a specific orientation.
concepts.content: Two band-pass filters are said to be in quadrature if the impulse responses are Hilbert transform pairs along some orientation in the frequency domain. Sine and cosine functions of the same frequency are Hilbert transform pairs, as are sine and cosine phase Gabor functions, of the same frequency and Gaussian envelope parameters. Thus, these filter pairs are also quadrature pairs. When convolving two filters in quadrature with a signal (or image) the two outputs are also in quadrature.
concepts.motivation_md: Using quadrature pairs allows for the extraction of signal energy (amplitude) that is smooth and does not oscillate at the frequency of the carrier signal.
concepts.recap_md:
- Filters are in quadrature if their impulse responses form a Hilbert transform pair. 
- Common examples include sine/cosine pairs and Gabor filter pairs. 
- Convolving a signal with quadrature filters results in outputs that are also in quadrature.

concepts.title: Gabor Functions as Quadrature Pairs
concepts.one_liner: Gabor functions approximate quadrature pairs only when the spatial spread $\sigma$ is sufficiently large.
concepts.content: The quadrature in the Gabor functions is an approximation that only holds for $\sigma$ sufficiently large. For small $\sigma$ the filter does not form a quadrature pair. For large $\sigma$, the real and imaginary parts of the Gabor filter (cosine and sine phase local filters) are filters in quadrature with the vector $n=(u_0,v_0)$ pointing in the direction of the central frequency of the Gabor function.
concepts.motivation_md: Understanding this approximation is critical for designing Gabor filters that accurately measure local phase and energy without introducing artifacts from DC components.
concepts.recap_md:
- Gabor quadrature is an approximation dependent on the filter's $\sigma$. 
- Large $\sigma$ values are required for the sine and cosine components to behave as a true quadrature pair. 
- The quadrature direction is determined by the central frequency vector of the Gabor function.

concepts.title: Aliasing in Generative Image Models
concepts.one_liner: Aliasing is a common source of artifacts in generative image models, particularly during upsampling stages.
concepts.content: Aliasing is often a source of image artifacts in generative image models. One example is generative adversarial networks where images are produced as a sequence of learned convolutions and upsampling stages. When the upsampling operations are done without paying attention to aliasing, the output images show a number of artifacts. Those artifacts can be removed by carefully implementing each stage to avoid aliasing.
concepts.motivation_md: Generative models like GANs often produce "checkerboard" or other unnatural patterns; identifying aliasing as the cause allows researchers to design better upsampling layers.
concepts.recap_md:
- Generative models often suffer from artifacts due to poorly implemented upsampling.
- Artifacts in GANs can be mitigated by designing stages that explicitly avoid aliasing.
- Careful implementation of convolutions and upsampling is required for high-quality image synthesis.

concepts.title: Introduction to Filter Banks
concepts.one_liner: Filter banks use sets of filters and nonlinear operators to extract complex information from images.
concepts.content: Although linear filters can perform a wide range of operations, image understanding requires nonlinear operators. Sets of filters can be used to extract information about images, forming representations that help to understand the power of modern deep neural networks. Simple nonlinearities applied to the output of linear filters, such as the squaring nonlinearity, can be used to build useful image representations.
concepts.motivation_md: Linear filters alone are insufficient for complex image understanding; filter banks provide a way to capture multi-scale and multi-orientation features using nonlinear combinations.
concepts.recap_md:

- Filter banks are traditional tools for building image representations.
- Nonlinearities like squaring are applied to filter outputs to extract meaningful features.

concepts.title: Motivation for Gabor Filters
concepts.one_liner: Gabor filters provide a way to perform localized frequency analysis, overcoming the global nature of the Fourier transform.
concepts.content:
The Fourier transform allows us to extract frequency, amplitude, and phase information, but only globally. For this information to be useful in image analysis, it needs to be localized. While image gradients provide localized orientation information, Gabor filters represent another family of filters used for localized image analysis. 

A standard sine function has infinite support; therefore, a single Fourier coefficient (obtained via scalar product) does not provide information about local structures within an image. To achieve localized analysis, one must restrict the spatial support of the sinusoidal basis function. This is achieved by taking the product of a Gaussian function, which has local support and desirable properties, and a sine or cosine wave. The resulting profile is called a Gabor filter, introduced by Dennis Gabor in 1946.
concepts.motivation_md: Standard Fourier analysis fails to tell us *where* a frequency occurs; Gabor filters solve this by windowing the sinusoid with a Gaussian, enabling simultaneous localization in both space and frequency.
concepts.recap_md:
- Fourier analysis is global, but image features like orientation need to be localized.
- Sinusoids have infinite support, making them poor for local feature detection.
- Gabor filters localize frequency analysis by multiplying a sinusoid with a Gaussian window.

concepts.title: Computing Local Amplitude
concepts.one_liner: The squared local amplitude is computed as the sum of the squared outputs of two band-pass filters in quadrature.
concepts.content:
Let $h(x,y)$ and $q(x,y)$ be band-pass filters in quadrature, and let $\ell_h(x,y)$ and $\ell_q(x,y)$ be the result of convolving the signal $\ell(x,y)$ with $h(x,y)$ and $q(x,y)$, respectively. Then, the squared local amplitude is a measure of the image power within the frequency bandwidth of the filters in the local neighborhood of $(x,y)$:

$$a^2(x,y) = \ell_h ^2 (x,y) + \ell_q ^2 (x,y)$$

(see figure: Computation of localized amplitude. The input is filtered by a pair of quadrature Gabor filters. Each filter output is squared and the result is added.)

This computation can be viewed as a two-layer convolutional neural network with two channels in the first layer, a squaring nonlinearity, and a sum in the second layer. This simple system can perform a number of interesting operations.
concepts.motivation_md: Local amplitude provides a measure of image power within a specific frequency band at a specific location. It is a fundamental operation for detecting features like edges and textures while remaining invariant to certain signal changes.

- Local amplitude is calculated by squaring and summing the outputs of quadrature filter pairs.
 - It measures local image power within the filters' frequency bandwidth.
 - The process can be modeled as a simple two-layer convolutional neural network.

concepts.title: Sign Invariance of Local Amplitude
concepts.one_liner: Local amplitude is sign invariant, meaning the output remains the same even if the input image contrast is inverted.
concepts.content:
The local amplitude of a signal is independent of the contrast sign of the input image. For a delta function $\ell(x,y) = \delta(x,y)$ filtered by cosine and sine phase Gabor filters, the local amplitude is the Gaussian envelope of the Gabor function:

$$\begin{split}
a(x,y)  & = \sqrt{\ell_h ^2 (x,y) + \ell_q ^2 (x,y)}  \\ 
 & = \sqrt{\psi^2_r(x,y;u_0,v_0) + \psi^2_i(x,y;u_0,v_0)}  \\
 & = \frac{1}{2\pi \sigma^2} \exp{\left(-\frac{x^2 + y^2}{2 \sigma^2} \right)}
\end{split}$$

If the input is $\ell(x,y) = -\delta(x,y)$, the amplitude image does not change, demonstrating sign invariance. As shown in (see figure: Examples of Gabor outputs to illustrate the contrast invariances present in the local amplitude. In these examples the Gabor filters are centered along the horizontal frequency axis ($v_0=0$)...), the local amplitude of two impulses of opposite signs results in two identical Gaussians. 

This property is especially useful for localizing edges. For an image composed of squares with different polarities relative to the background, the local amplitude provides a boundary detector invariant to those polarity changes. While the local amplitude detects the boundaries, the differences between the squares are encoded in the local phase.
concepts.motivation_md: Sign invariance allows feature detectors (like edge detectors) to respond consistently to a boundary regardless of whether it transitions from light-to-dark or dark-to-light.

- Local amplitude is sign invariant, producing the same output for positive and negative versions of an input.
 - For a Gabor filter, the local amplitude of a delta function is simply the Gaussian envelope.
 - This property enables robust edge detection across varying polarities and contrasts.

concepts.title: Filter Bank
concepts.one_liner: A filter bank is a collection of filters used to extract different image features for building a representation.
concepts.content: A filter bank is a collection of filters, each tuned to extract a different image feature, and used to build an image representation.
concepts.motivation_md: A single filter can only capture one type of feature; a bank of filters allows a system to analyze an image across multiple scales, orientations, and frequencies simultaneously.
concepts.recap_md:
- A filter bank consists of multiple filters.
 - Each filter is tuned to a specific image feature.
 - The collective outputs form a comprehensive image representation.

concepts.title: Gabor Filter Bank
concepts.one_liner: A Gabor filter bank uses sets of Gabor filters selective to different spatial frequencies to cover the frequency domain.
concepts.content:
2D Gabor filters are selective in spatial frequency. It is very useful to work with sets of Gabor filters, each selective to a different spatial frequency so that they cover the full space of spatial frequencies.

(see figure: Examples of Gabor sets. Two different ways of tiling the frequency domain.)

There are different arrangements for these sets. One approach uses a rectangular grid to sample the frequency domain, where all functions share the same Gaussian width $\sigma$. Another approach uses a polar arrangement where the Gaussian width $\sigma$ is proportional to the distance between the central frequency and the origin. This polar arrangement produces filters that are rotated and scaled versions of each other.
concepts.motivation_md: To fully analyze an image, one needs to capture information at all orientations and scales. Gabor filter banks provide a structured way to tile the frequency domain to ensure no information is missed.
concepts.recap_md:
- Gabor filter banks tile the frequency domain using multiple selective filters.
 - Rectangular arrangements use a fixed $\sigma$ across a grid.
 - Polar arrangements scale $\sigma$ with frequency, creating a multi-scale representation.

concepts.title: Gabor Transform
concepts.one_liner: The Gabor transform is a variation of the Fourier transform performed by varying the central frequency of a Gabor function.
concepts.content:
Convolution with a Gabor function is equivalent to performing a Fourier transform on an image after applying a Gaussian window:

$$\begin{split}
\ell_{\psi} \left(x,y,u,v \right)  & =   \iint \ell\left(x',y'\right) \psi(x-x',y-y';u,v) \, dx' dy' = \\
& = \iint  \ell\left(x',y'\right) g(x-x',y-y') \exp \left( j \left(u (x-x') + v (y-y') \right) \right) dx' dy' = \\
\end{split}$$

By extracting terms independent of $(x',y')$ and using the symmetry of the Gaussian window, we obtain:

$$\begin{split}
& = \exp \left( j \left(u x + v y \right) \right) \iint \ell\left(x',y'\right) g(x'-x,y'-y) \exp \left(- j \left(u x' + v y' \right) \right) dx' dy'
\end{split}$$

The Gabor transform is obtained when we vary the central frequency $(u,v)$ of the Gabor function. Note that the Gabor transform is not self-inverting.
concepts.motivation_md: Standard Fourier transforms lose spatial information. The Gabor transform provides a localized frequency analysis, showing which frequencies are present at specific locations in an image.
concepts.recap_md:
- The Gabor transform is a windowed Fourier transform using a Gaussian window.
 - It is computed by varying the central frequency $(u,v)$ of the Gabor kernel.
 - Unlike the standard Fourier transform, the Gabor transform is not self-inverting.

concepts.title: Motivation for Steerable Filters
concepts.one_liner: The motivation for steerable filters is the need to efficiently rotate oriented filters and interpolate between a fixed number of filter outputs.
concepts.content:
A key question with oriented filters is how to change their orientation efficiently. Specifically, given a filter $h(x,y)$, we want to transform it into a continuous function $h(x,y, \theta)$ where $\theta$ specifies the rotation. 

In the case of Gabor filters, each orientation typically requires a separate convolution. This raises the question of whether we must create a new Gabor function for every orientation, or if we can interpolate between a fixed number of predefined oriented filter outputs. Determining the necessary number of orientation samples is a central problem.
concepts.motivation_md: Convolving an image with many different oriented filters is computationally expensive. Steerable filters allow us to synthesize a filter at any orientation from a small basis set of filters.
concepts.recap_md:
- Oriented filters need a way to be rotated continuously by an angle $\theta$.
 - The goal is to interpolate between a fixed number of filter outputs rather than re-convolving for every angle.
 - This leads to the question of how many discrete orientations must be sampled.

concepts.title: Orientation Sampling Theorem
concepts.one_liner: The orientation sampling theorem determines how many discrete orientation samples are needed to interpolate a filter at any arbitrary orientation.
concepts.content: The orientation sampling theorem is a generalization of the Nyquist sampling theorem applied to the dimension of orientation rather than space. It addresses whether, given a certain number of discrete samples in orientation, one can interpolate between those samples to synthesize the output of a filter at an arbitrary, intermediate orientation. The answer is affirmative, and the specific number of filter samples required for perfect interpolation depends on the mathematical form of the filter.
concepts.motivation_md: Just as the Nyquist theorem tells us how often to sample in time or space, this theorem tells us how many orientations we need to sample to perfectly reconstruct the angular information of a filter.
concepts.recap_md:
- It is a generalization of the Nyquist sampling theorem for the orientation dimension.
 - It allows for the synthesis of filters at arbitrary orientations from discrete samples.
 - The required number of samples is determined by the specific form of the filter.

concepts.title: Spatiotemporal Gabor Filters
concepts.one_liner: Spatiotemporal Gabor filters generalize 2D spatial Gabor functions to 3D $x-y-t$ functions for motion analysis.
concepts.content:
### Spatiotemporal Gabor Filters

Just as we did with Gaussian derivatives, extending Gabor filters for motion analysis is a direct generalization of the $x-y$ 2D Gabor function to a $x-y-t$ 3D Gabor function. (see figure: Space-time Gabor filters. (a) Cosine and sine $x$-$t$ Gabor filter, and (b) the sketch of its transfer function. (c) Sketch of the transfer function of a spatiotemporal Gabor filter in two spatial...)

@fig-spacetimefilts (a) shows a $x-t$ (cosine and sine) Gabor function in one spatial dimension, and @fig-spacetimefilts (b) shows a sketch of its Fourier transform. This function is selective to signals translating to the right with a speed $v=1$, i.e. $\ell(x-t)$. The red line in @fig-spacetimefilts (b) shows the Dirac line that contains the energy of the moving signal.

In two spatial dimensions, @fig-spacetimefilts (c) shows the sketch of the Gabor transfer function. Note that the $x-y-t$ Gabor filter is not selective to velocity. If we have a 2D moving signal $\ell(x-v_xt, y-v_yt)$, the Fourier transform is contained inside a Dirac plane. Therefore, there are an infinite number of planes that will pass by the frequencies of the Gabor filter. All those planes intersect the red line shown in @fig-spacetimefilts (c). A single Gabor filter cannot disambiguate the input velocity.
concepts.motivation_md: To analyze motion in video, filters must account for time as a third dimension. Spatiotemporal Gabor filters extend spatial frequency analysis to the time domain, allowing the detection of signals moving at specific speeds and directions.
concepts.recap_md: - Spatiotemporal Gabor filters are 3D $x-y-t$ generalizations of 2D spatial Gabor functions.

concepts.title: Velocity-Tuned Filters
concepts.one_liner: Velocity-tuned filters combine quadrature pairs of space-time oriented filters to identify the motion speed and direction of a signal.
concepts.content:
### Velocity-Tuned Filters

We can use quadrature pairs of oriented filters in space-time to find motion speed and direction in the video signal. We just need to find the space-time orientation of strongest response. @fig-spacetimetiles2 (a) shows a set of Gabor filters sampling the space-time frequency domain. When the input contains a moving signal, we can use a set of filters to identify the plane in the Fourier domain that contains the input energy. @fig-spacetimetiles2 (b) shows the subset of filters that have the strongest output for a particular input motion.

(see figure: Two 3D plots in the frequency domain with axes $w_x$, $w_y$, and $w_t$. (a) shows a dense cubic grid of spheres representing a 3D spatiotemporal filter bank. (b) shows a subset of these spheres that...)

As an illustration, @fig-MT_velocity_tuned shows one possible architecture to create velocity-selective units. The first layer is composed by space-time Gabor filters (cosine and sine), which are frequency-selective units. Here we represent the impulse response of each filter by a small $x-y-t$ cube. For each quadrature pair we compute the amplitude. Then amplitude outputs are combined to form different planes in the Fourier domain to create velocity-selective outputs. A normalization layer can be added to normalize the outputs by dividing every output by the sum of all the amplitudes. The full architecture is nonlinear. Given an input sequence, one can estimate velocity by looking at the velocity-tuned unit with the strongest response.

concepts.title: Steering Equation for First-order Gaussian Derivatives
concepts.one_liner: The steering equation for the first derivative of a Gaussian filter allows synthesizing a directional derivative in any direction as a linear combination of horizontal and vertical derivatives.
concepts.content: A directional derivative in any direction can be synthesized as a linear combination of derivatives in the horizontal and vertical directions. By the linearity of convolution, this applies to the derivative applied to any filter or image. The steering equation for the first derivative of a Gaussian filter is $$g_{x}(x,y,	heta) = \cos(\theta) g_x(x,y) + \sin(\theta) g_y(x,y)$$ where $g_x$ and $g_y$ are the Gaussian derivatives along $x$ and $y$, and $g_{x}(x,y,\theta)$ is the derivative along the direction defined by the angle $\theta$. The interpolation functions are $k_1(\theta) = \cos(\theta)$ and $k_2(\theta) = \sin(\theta)$. A first-order derivative filter of any orientation can be synthesized from a linear combination of two basis filter derivatives.
concepts.motivation_md: It allows for the computation of image derivatives at any arbitrary orientation without having to re-convolve the image with a new filter for every angle, saving significant computation time.
concepts.recap_md: - A first-order Gaussian derivative at any angle $\theta$ is a linear combination of $x$ and $y$ derivatives. - The interpolation functions are $k_1(\theta) = \cos(\theta)$ and $k_2(\theta) = \sin(\theta)$.

concepts.title: Steering Equation for Second-order Gaussian Derivatives
concepts.one_liner: The steering equation for second-order Gaussian derivatives synthesizes a derivative at any orientation using a linear combination of three basis filters.
concepts.content: All higher order Gaussian derivatives have the property of being steerable, but the number of basis filters changes with the order. For second-order Gaussian derivatives, the steering equation is: $$\begin{split} g_{x,x}(x,y,\theta) & = g_{xx}(\cos(\theta) x - \sin (\theta) y, \sin(\theta) x + \cos (\theta)y) = \\ &= \cos^2(\theta) g_{xx}(x,y) + \sin^2(\theta) g_{yy}(x,y) - 2 \cos(\theta) \sin(\theta) g_{xy}(x,y) \end{split}$$ To interpolate the derivative along any orientation requires three basis filters and the interpolation functions are $k_1(\theta) = \cos^2(\theta)$, $k_2(\theta) = \sin^2(\theta)$, and $k_3(\theta) = -2\cos(\theta)\sin(\theta)$. The minus sign in $k_3$ is due to the positive direction of $\theta$ being counter-clockwise. A second-order derivative needs three basis filters.
concepts.motivation_md: Higher-order derivatives are needed for detecting features like ridges or blobs. Steering allows these features to be analyzed at any orientation using a fixed set of basis filters.
concepts.recap_md: - Second-order steering requires three basis filters: $g_{xx}$, $g_{yy}$, and $g_{xy}$. - The interpolation functions involve $\cos^2(\theta)$, $\sin^2(\theta)$, and $-2\cos(\theta)\sin(\theta)$.

concepts.title: Steerable Filter Architecture
concepts.one_liner: Steerable filter architecture uses a set of basis filters and gain maps to synthesize oriented filters at any position in an image.
concepts.content: This architecture for processing images with oriented steerable filters involves passing input images through a set of basis filters. The outputs of those filters are then modulated with a set of gain maps, which can be different at each pixel. These gain maps adjust the linear combinations of the basis filters, allowing the input filter to be steered to the desired orientations at each position. (see figure: Architecture for steerable filters. This architecture computes the second-order image derivative along orientation $\theta$.)
concepts.motivation_md: This architecture provides a computationally efficient way to apply filters at different orientations across an image, which is essential for tasks like edge detection and texture analysis.

concepts.one_liner: The Steering Theorem defines the conditions and number of basis filters required to synthesize a rotated version of a filter as a linear combination of its basis.
concepts.content: The Steering Theorem quantifies how many basis filters are required to steer a given filter, which depends on how sharply oriented the filter is. For a filter with impulse response $h(x,y)$, or $h(r,\phi)$ in polar coordinates, the steering condition is the requirement that the rotated filter, $h(r,\phi - \theta)$, be a linear combination of a set of basis filters that are rotated versions of itself, $h(r,\phi - \theta_m)$ with $m \in (1,M)$: $$h(r,\phi - \theta) = \sum_{m=1}^{M} k_{m}(\theta) h(r,\phi - \theta_m) .$$ If the filter is expressed as a Fourier series in angle, $h(r,\phi) = \sum_{n=-N}^{N} a_n(r) \exp \left( j n \phi \right)$, the steering condition holds if and only if the interpolation functions $k_{j}(\theta)$ are solutions of: $$\left[ \begin{array}{c} 1 \\ \exp (j \theta) \\ \ldots \\ \exp (j N \theta) \\ \end{array} \right] = \left[ \begin{array}{cccc} 1 & 1 & \ldots & 1 \\ \exp (j \theta_{1}) & \exp (j \theta_{2}) & \ldots & \exp (j \theta_{M}) \\ \vdots & \vdots & \vdots & \vdots \\ \exp (j N \theta_{1}) & \exp (j N \theta_{2}) & \ldots & \exp (j N \theta_{M}) \end{array} \right] \left[ \begin{array}{c} k_{1}(\theta) \\ k_{2}(\theta) \\ \vdots \\ k_{M}(\theta) \end{array} \right].$$
concepts.motivation_md: This theorem provides the mathematical foundation for steerable filters, determining the minimum number of basis filters needed to perfectly reconstruct a filter at any orientation.
concepts.recap_md: - Relates the number of basis filters to the angular frequency content of the filter. - Provides a matrix equation to solve for the interpolation functions $k_m(\theta)$.

concepts.title: Optimality of Gabor Localization
concepts.one_liner: Gabor functions are the optimal functions for achieving the best simultaneous localization in both the spatial and frequency domains.
concepts.content: Gabor functions are localized in both the spatial and frequency domain. One remarkable property of the Gabor function is that it is the optimal function that achieves the best simultaneous localization in space and frequency.
concepts.motivation_md: In signal processing, there is a fundamental trade-off between resolution in time (or space) and resolution in frequency. Gabor functions are significant because they mathematically reach the lower bound of this uncertainty principle, providing the most precise possible representation across both domains.
concepts.recap_md: - Gabor functions provide simultaneous localization in space and frequency.

concepts.title: 2D Complex Gabor Function
concepts.one_liner: A 2D complex Gabor function is formed by multiplying a complex Fourier basis function by a spatially localized 2D Gaussian window.
concepts.content:
Gabor functions can be extended to two dimensions by using 2D Gaussians and waves. Using complex waves provides a more general form of the Gabor function. We can multiply a complex Fourier basis function, $\exp{ \left(j  \left(u_0 x + v_0 y \right)  \right)}$, by a spatially localized 2D Gaussian window, $\exp{\left(-\frac{x^2 + y^2}{2 \sigma^2} \right) }$ to obtain a Gabor function, $\psi(x,y)$:
$$\psi(x,y;u_0,v_0) = \frac{1}{2\pi \sigma^2} \exp{\left(-\frac{x^2 + y^2}{2 \sigma^2} \right)} \exp{ \left( j \left(u_0 x + v_0 y \right) \right)}$$
concepts.motivation_md: While simple sinusoids have perfect frequency localization but no spatial localization, and Gaussians have spatial localization but poor frequency specificity, the complex Gabor function combines both to analyze specific frequencies at specific locations in an image.
concepts.recap_md: - The 2D Gabor function is the product of a 2D Gaussian and a complex exponential.

concepts.title: Cosine and Sine Phase Gabor Filters
concepts.one_liner: The real and imaginary components of a complex Gabor function define the cosine and sine phase Gabor filters, respectively.

A complex Gabor function is a complex-valued function of location and frequency. We can get the cosine and sine waves by looking at the real and imaginary components, $\psi(x,y;u_0,v_0) =  \psi_r(x,y;u_0,v_0) + j \psi_i(x,y;u_0,v_0)$ with:

$$\psi_i(x,y;u_0,v_0) = \frac{1}{2\pi \sigma^2} \exp{\left(-\frac{x^2 + y^2}{2 \sigma^2} \right)} \sin{ \left(u_0 x + v_0 y \right) }$$

concepts.title: Gabor Filter Parameters
concepts.one_liner: The Gabor filter's behavior is determined by its central frequency, which sets orientation, and its width, which determines spatial locality.
concepts.content:
The Gabor function changes when modifying its parameters: the central frequency $(u_0,v_0)$ and the width $\sigma$. The value of $\sigma$ sets the locality of the window of analysis, while the values of $(u_0,v_0)$ adjust the orientation and frequency of the Gabor function. A large $\sigma$ makes the spatial extent large and the frequency extent small; a small value of $\sigma$ has the opposite behavior. Analyzing an image with a set of Gabor functions with a large $\sigma$ is similar to computing the Fourier transform of the image.

concepts.title: Biological Motivation for Gabor Filters
concepts.one_liner: Gabor filters are motivated by their similarity to cortical receptive fields in the mammalian visual system.
concepts.content: One important characteristic of Gabor filters is that they are very similar to the shape of some cortical receptive fields found in the mammalian visual system. This similarity suggests that these filters are an effective way to build image representations, reflecting the simple and complex cells found in the visual system.
concepts.motivation_md: Computer vision often looks to biological systems for efficient ways to process visual information. Since mammalian brains use Gabor-like structures to process scenes, using them in algorithms is a biologically-inspired approach to feature detection.
concepts.recap_md: - Gabor filters mimic the receptive fields of simple cells in the mammalian primary visual cortex.

concepts.title: Convolution with Gabor Filters
concepts.one_liner: Convolving an image with a Gabor filter produces an output that represents the image's content at a specific location, frequency, and orientation.
concepts.content:
The convolution of the Gabor function with an image, $\ell(x,y)$, results in an output image that depends on both space, $(x,y)$, and frequency, $(u,v)$:
$$\ell_{\psi} \left(x,y,u,v \right) = \ell\left(x,y\right) \circ \psi(x,y;u,v)$$

concepts.title: Steering Rule for Polynomials
concepts.one_liner: For an $N$-th order polynomial with even or odd symmetry, $N+1$ basis functions are sufficient for steering when combined with radially symmetric window functions.
concepts.content: Sometimes it is more convenient to think of filters as polynomials multiplied by radially symmetric window functions, which is the case for high-order Gaussian derivatives. For an $N$-th order polynomial with even or odd symmetry, $N+1$ basis functions are sufficient to achieve steerability.
concepts.motivation_md: This rule provides a clear mathematical bound on the number of basis functions required to steer a filter, simplifying the design of steerable filters for complex shapes like high-order derivatives.
concepts.recap_md:
- Filters can be represented as polynomials times radially symmetric window functions.
 - An $N$-th order symmetric polynomial requires only $N+1$ basis functions for steering.

concepts.title: Steerability Sampling Invariance
concepts.one_liner: Steerability is preserved after sampling because spatial sampling and the weighted summation of basis functions are interchangeable operations.
concepts.content: Although steerability is typically derived in the continuous domain, it is a property that still holds after sampling the filter function. This is because spatial sampling and steerability are interchangeable: the weighted sum of spatially sampled functions is equal to the spatial sampling of the same weighted sum of continuous basis functions.
concepts.motivation_md: This ensures that steerable filter theory, which is often developed for continuous functions, remains mathematically valid when implemented on discrete digital grids.

concepts.title: Separable Basis Filters for Steering
concepts.one_liner: Using $x-y$ separable functions as basis filters improves computational efficiency for steering operations.
concepts.content: For computational efficiency, it is more convenient to have the basis filters all be $x-y$ separable functions. concepts.title: Steerable Quadrature Pairs
concepts.one_liner: Steerable quadrature pairs are filter sets that allow for arbitrary shifts in both orientation and phase.
concepts.content: As in the case of Gabor filters, it is useful to build quadrature pairs of steerable filters. Steerable-quadrature filters allow for arbitrary shifts both in orientation and in phase.
concepts.motivation_md: These pairs are essential for analyzing local image structure independently of phase, which is useful for tasks like edge and line detection where the exact position relative to the filter center may vary.

 - They are analogous to Gabor filters but designed within the steerable filter framework.

concepts.title: Hilbert Transform Steerable Approximation
concepts.one_liner: The Hilbert transform of a second-order Gaussian derivative can be approximated using a third-order odd polynomial to create a steerable quadrature pair.
concepts.content:
Consider the second-order derivatives of a Gaussian with $\sigma^2=1/2$, normalized so that the integral over all space of its squared magnitude equals 1:

$$\begin{split}
g_{xx}(x,y) &= 0.9213(2x^2-1) \exp \left(-(x^2+y^2) \right) \\
g_{xy}(x,y) &= 1.843 (x y) \exp \left(-(x^2+y^2) \right) \\
g_{yy}(x,y) &= 0.9213(2y^2-1) \exp \left(-(x^2+y^2) \right)
\end{split}$$

It is possible to get a good approximation to its Hilbert transform using a Gaussian times a third-order odd polynomial. The approximation to the Hilbert transform of $g_{xx}(x,y)$ is:

$$h_{xx}(x,y) = -0.9780 (-2.254 x+x^3) \exp \left(-(x^2+y^2) \right)$$

where $g_{xx}(x,y)$ and its Hilbert transform $h_{xx}(x,y)$ have the same spectral content but opposite phase. (see figure: Quadrature pair, $g_{xx} \left[n,m \right)$ and $h_{xx} \left[n,m \right]$. The filters are sampled in space and cropped into a window of $13\times13$ pixels.] To steer $h_{xx}(x,y)$ to an angle $\theta$, this approximation requires four basis functions, rather than three as for the second-order derivative of a Gaussian. The other three functions needed are:

$$\begin{split}
h_2(x,y) &= -0.9780(-0.7515+x^2) y \exp \left(-(x^2+y^2) \right) \\
h_3(x,y) &= -0.9780(-0.7515+y^2) x \exp \left(-(x^2+y^2) \right) \\
h_4(x,y) &= -0.9780 (-2.254 y+y^3) \exp \left(-(x^2+y^2) \right) 
\end{split}$$
concepts.motivation_md: Since the exact Hilbert transform of a Gaussian derivative is not steerable with a finite basis, this polynomial approximation allows for the practical implementation of steerable quadrature pairs.
concepts.recap_md:
- The Hilbert transform of $g_{xx}$ is approximated by a third-order odd polynomial times a Gaussian.
 - Steering the approximated Hilbert transform requires a set of four basis functions.

concepts.title: Non-uniqueness of Steerable Basis Functions
concepts.one_liner: Steerable basis functions are not unique; a space can be spanned by different sets, such as $x-y$ separable filters or rotated versions of the same function.
concepts.content: The basis functions for steerability are not unique. For instance, the space spanning all rotations of $g_{xx}$ can be represented by $x-y$ separable filters ($g_{xx}$, $g_{xy}$, and $g_{yy}$) or by three rotated versions of $g_{xx}$ at 0, 60, and 120 degrees. The latter is a non-separable basis spanning the same space as the separable filters. Similarly, different basis functions can span all rotations of $h_{xx}$. Spatial scaling of these filters results in changing the parameter $\sigma$. (see figure: (a) Second derivative of Gaussian, $x-y$ separable steerable basis set. b) Approximation to Hilbert transform of second derivative of Gaussian, $x-y$ steerable basis set. (c) Nonseparable basis equivalent to (a). (d) Nonseparable basis set equivalent to (b).)
concepts.motivation_md: Understanding non-uniqueness allows designers to choose basis sets that optimize for specific criteria, such as computational efficiency through separability or geometric intuition through rotated versions.
concepts.recap_md:
- Multiple different sets of basis functions can span the same space of rotated filters.
 - Common choices include $x-y$ separable sets or sets of rotated versions of the primary filter.

concepts.title: Oriented Energy
concepts.one_liner: Oriented energy is calculated as the sum of the squared responses of a steerable quadrature pair at a specific angle.
concepts.content: (see figure: (a) Second derivative of Gaussian, $x-y$ separable steerable basis set. b) Approximation to Hilbert transform of second derivative of Gaussian, $x-y$ steerable basis set. (c) Nonseparable basis equivalent to (a). (d) Nonseparable basis set equivalent to (b).) Oriented energy can be computed as a function of angle $\theta$, for all angles, from the basis filter responses. Using the $g_{xx}$ and $h_{xx}$ filters, the oriented energy is defined as: $$E(x,y,\theta) = g_{xx}(x,y,\theta)^2 + h_{xx}(x,y,\theta)^2$$
concepts.motivation_md: Oriented energy provides a phase-invariant measure of local image structure, allowing for the detection of edges and lines regardless of their specific intensity profile or polarity.
concepts.recap_md:
- Oriented energy is the sum of squared responses from even and odd phase steerable filters.
 - It allows for the continuous calculation of energy across all possible orientations.

concepts.title: Oriented Energy Cross-terms
concepts.one_liner: When multiple oriented structures exist within a filter's passband, squaring the responses introduces cross-terms that prevent simple linear superposition of energies.
concepts.content: Polar plots of oriented energy as a function of angle can reveal artifacts at intersections when using $g_{xx}$ and $h_{xx}$ filters. This issue is not due to insufficient angular resolution, but rather a non-linear interaction. When there are two oriented structures within the passband of the quadrature pair filters, the sum of the energies of the individual structures is not the same as the energy of the sum of the structures. (see figure: (Polar plots of orientation energy as a function of angle, computed using $g_{xx}$, $h_{xx}$ filters. (a) Note the non-superposition of oriented energies near the junction of the two lines. (b)...) Because energy is found by squaring, the combination of multiple structures is not linear. When two oriented structures are within the passband, the convolution in the Fourier domain picks up extra cross-terms from the interaction between the structures, in addition to the desired terms from squaring individual frequency responses.
concepts.motivation_md: Recognizing the presence of cross-terms is crucial for interpreting oriented energy plots, as it explains why energy may not perfectly represent the sum of independent components in complex regions like junctions.
concepts.recap_md:
- Squaring filter responses to find energy makes the combination of multiple structures non-linear.
 - Interaction between structures in the filter passband creates cross-terms in the Fourier domain.

prereq.rationale: Steerable filters are motivated by the computational inefficiency of using many Gabor filters at different orientations.
The architecture is defined by the use of a fixed set of basis filters.
Gain maps are the mechanism used in the architecture to steer the filters at each pixel.
The Steering Theorem provides the mathematical framework and solutions for the steering condition.
Steerable quadrature pairs extend the concept of quadrature phase to oriented filters.
Quadrature pairs are often constructed using a filter and its Hilbert transform.
Oriented energy is defined as the sum of squared responses from a steerable quadrature pair.
Velocity-tuned filters are constructed from a bank of spatiotemporal Gabor filters that sample the space-time frequency domain.
The technique uses quadrature pairs of oriented filters to detect the speed and direction of motion.

overlay.rationale: Second-order steering builds on the concept of synthesizing derivatives from basis filters introduced with first-order derivatives.
The steering condition formalizes the goal of synthesizing rotated filters mentioned in the motivation.
This rule provides a specific instance of the number of basis functions required for polynomial filters under the general theorem.
This technique provides a practical way to construct steerable quadrature pairs using Gaussian derivatives.
This concept clarifies that the set of basis filters used for steering is not unique and can be represented in multiple ways.
Cross-terms explain why simple energy superposition fails in complex junctions, complicating the basic oriented energy model.
Low-pass filtering is a technique used to mitigate the artifacts caused by cross-terms in energy calculations.
Spatiotemporal Gabor filters are a direct generalization of the 2D spatial Gabor function to a 3D x-y-t function.
